sections.Disease management: CV, infection, neurology, respiratory, renal, GI, and other systemic disease (haem/endocrine/toxicology/obstetric).

sections.Practical procedures: Respiratory, cardiovascular, CNS, and other practical procedures.
sections.General patient care: Resuscitation, comfort & recovery, patient safety, and end of life.

questions.question: On day 4 after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, sedation is fully weaned. A 60-year-old man opens his eyes to his name and follows simple commands consistently. However, he has prominent, stimulus-sensitive myoclonic jerks of all four limbs that worsen with intentional movement. EEG shows no epileptiform activity. What is the MOST accurate interpretation?
questions.explanation: Lance-Adams syndrome is post-anoxic action myoclonus occurring in a conscious, aware, command-following patient — the key feature distinguishing it from myoclonic status epilepticus, in which consciousness is absent and EEG shows epileptiform activity. Unlike myoclonic status epilepticus, which carries an essentially universally poor prognosis, Lance-Adams syndrome can have a favourable outcome with treatment (levetiracetam, clonazepam, or piracetam). Clinicians must recognise this entity to avoid premature withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment.
options: Post-anoxic myoclonus always indicates cortical spreading depolarisation and mandates ICP monitoring
Myoclonus in this context indicates severe cerebellar injury and has no specific treatment implication
The combination of command-following and myoclonus is contradictory; the command-following responses are reflexive rather than voluntary
This represents myoclonic status epilepticus; immediate antiepileptic therapy and withdrawal of active care are appropriate given the universally poor prognosis
This is Lance-Adams syndrome (post-anoxic action myoclonus); the patient is conscious and aware, and prognosis may be favourable with appropriate treatment

questions.question: The NUTRIREA-2 trial randomised critically ill patients on vasopressors to full-calorie EN versus a restrictive EN strategy. What were the main results?
questions.explanation: NUTRIREA-2 (Reignier, NEJM 2018) randomised 2410 critically ill adults on vasopressors and mechanical ventilation to full-calorie EN (20 kcal/kg/day) versus restrictive EN (targeting 6 kcal/kg/day, approximately 500 mL/day of water). The primary outcome — 28-day mortality — was not significantly different between groups (37.0% vs 37.0%). However, patients receiving full-calorie EN had significantly more GI complications including vomiting, diarrhoea, bowel ischaemia, colonic pseudo-obstruction, and digestive haemorrhage. This suggests that attempting to meet full caloric targets via EN in haemodynamically unstable patients may cause harm.
options: Full-calorie EN significantly reduced 28-day mortality in vasopressor-dependent patients and should be recommended as standard of care in haemodynamically unstable critically ill patients
Restrictive EN significantly reduced ICU-acquired infections compared with full-calorie EN in shock
No significant mortality difference was found; full-calorie EN was associated with more GI complications including vomiting and bowel ischaemia
Full-calorie EN was safe and should be recommended in all haemodynamically stable patients on vasopressors
The trial was stopped early because full-calorie EN caused unacceptable rates of bowel ischaemia

questions.question: A ventilated COPD patient's PaCO2 is 72 mmHg and pH 7.28 after implementing controlled hypoventilation. A colleague insists on aggressively correcting PaCO2 to 40 mmHg by increasing minute ventilation. Why is this approach potentially harmful?
questions.explanation: Aggressive correction of hypercapnia in mechanically ventilated COPD patients carries significant risk. COPD patients often have pre-existing metabolic alkalosis from chronic CO2 retention, so rapidly correcting PaCO2 can cause life-threatening alkalemia. More critically, increasing minute ventilation to correct PaCO2 worsens dynamic hyperinflation by shortening expiratory time — the very mechanism causing respiratory failure. The recommended approach (permissive hypercapnia) accepts pH above 7.2, provided there is no intracranial hypertension or overt haemodynamic instability. The therapeutic goal is to move pH towards normal, not to achieve a target PaCO2. With appropriate bronchodilation and hyperinflation reduction, PaCO2 often improves over time without requiring aggressive ventilatory adjustments.
questions.section: Part IV: Ventilatory Support and Mechanics
options: Accept acidemia to pH 7.2 (permissive hypercapnia); the goal is to normalise pH direction, not PaCO2; increasing minute ventilation worsens dynamic hyperinflation

Rapidly normalise PaCO2 to 40 mmHg by increasing both respiratory rate and tidal volume simultaneously, accepting the transient increase in peak airway pressures as a necessary consequence of adequate CO2 clearance

Immediately administer a sodium bicarbonate infusion to normalise arterial pH while maintaining very low minute ventilation settings to minimise any further dynamic hyperinflation from ventilator-delivered breaths
Rapid correction eliminates the hypercapnic respiratory drive, causing the patient to stop triggering the ventilator
Correcting PaCO2 to normal in COPD patients triggers acute cor pulmonale from sudden changes in pulmonary vascular resistance

questions.question: A 53 year old male with end-stage renal disease underwent a renal transplant 6 months ago. Induction therapy was with Alemtuzumab and he is maintained on Tacrolimus and Mycophenolate mofetil. He presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with malaise, fever, cough and shortness of breath of 3 weeks duration. On arrival to ED, in addition to his immune suppression medications he was on sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim for Pneumocystis Jirovecii (PCP) prophylaxis and had received ganciclovir for 3 months after transplantation. He was diagnosed with CMV Pneumonia. Which was the main factor contributing to this infection?
questions.explanation: CMV-seronegative patients receiving a solid organ transplant from a CMV-seropositive donor are at the highest risk of primary CMV disease, from reactivation of latent virus transmitted in the allograft; being seropositive before transplant and receiving an organ from a seronegative donor is instead associated with lower risk. The net state of immunosuppression — influenced by the dose, duration and type of immunosuppressive agents, innate and adaptive host immune defects, age and comorbidities — also matters, and lymphocyte-depleting agents such as alemtuzumab (anti-CD52 antibody) are associated with increased CMV risk. CMV prophylaxis with ganciclovir should be continued for at least 6 months post-solid organ transplant, which significantly reduces CMV incidence; in this patient, stopping prophylaxis after only 3 months is the most likely main reason for the CMV pneumonia.
options: History of end stage renal disease
The patient was CMV seropositive prior to his transplant
The donor was CMV seronegative
Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim therapy
Ganciclovir was stopped after 3 months

questions.question: Regarding vasopressor therapy in septic shock:
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor agent recommended in septic shock. Dopamine may be considered as an alternative to norepinephrine specifically in selected patients with relative bradycardia and a low risk of tachyarrhythmia, based on SOAP II trial data — it is the only guideline-recognised alternative in this narrow context. The claim that low-dose 'renal-dose' dopamine is recommended as a renoprotective strategy in patients with acute kidney injury is false — this has been disproven in multiple trials and is explicitly not recommended for renal perfusion or protection. The claim that vasopressin is recommended as first-line therapy to be initiated concurrently with norepinephrine from the outset is also false — vasopressin is an adjunctive, norepinephrine-sparing agent added only once norepinephrine doses escalate, not a first-line concurrent agent.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Low-dose dopamine is recommended as a renoprotective strategy in septic shock patients with acute kidney injury.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Dopamine may be considered as an alternative to norepinephrine in selected patients with relative bradycardia and a low risk of tachyarrhythmia.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor agent recommended in septic shock.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Vasopressin is recommended as first-line vasopressor therapy to be initiated concurrently with norepinephrine from the outset of septic shock management.

questions.question: Regarding neutropenic patients, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE.
questions.explanation: Severe neutropenia is usually defined as an absolute neutrophil count below 500 cells/uL, not 1500. Fever in neutropenic patients is defined as a single oral temperature measurement above 38.3C, or a temperature of 38C or above sustained over a one-hour period (two measurements), not a single measurement above 38.5C. Relevant HSV infections in neutropenic patients are mostly due to reactivation of latent infection in seropositive patients rather than primo-infection, with likelihood influenced by chemotherapy's impact on cytotoxic T-lymphocytes; the listed HSV manifestations (oral/oesophageal ulcers, encephalitis, myelitis, pneumonia, hepatitis) are themselves accurate. Neutropenic patients with fever who have received CAR-T cell therapy within the preceding 2 months are indeed considered high risk. Conventional chest radiographs are less sensitive than high-resolution CT for showing abnormalities, so in neutropenic patients with signs of a lower respiratory tract infection, CT of the chest is the diagnostic method of choice even with a normal radiograph.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Neutropenic patients with fever who have received CAR-T cell therapy within the past 2 months are considered high risk.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Relevant HSV infections in neutropenic patients are mostly primo-infections and can lead to oral or oesophageal ulcera as well as organ manifestation such as encephalitis, myelitis, pneumonia and hepatitis.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Severe neutropenia is usually defined as an absolute neutrophil count <1500 cells/uL.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In a neutropenic patient with cough and a normal conventional chest radiograph, the additional benefit of a high-resolution CT scan of the chest is negligible.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Fever in a neutropenic patient is a common complication and is defined as a temperature >38.5C.

questions.question: A 66-year-old woman arrives at the emergency department after a syncopal episode. She is awake with a blood pressure of 110/75 mmHg. She is on chronic citalopram for depression, and blood tests reveal hypokalaemia. She suddenly becomes unresponsive and pulseless; the immediate ECG shows torsades de pointes. How do you manage this?
questions.explanation: For a pulseless patient with torsades de pointes, immediate defibrillation is required since this is a shockable rhythm; the polymorphic nature of the rhythm can prevent reliable synchronisation, so cardioversion may not always be possible. Drugs that prolong the QT interval - including amiodarone and procainamide - are dangerous and must be avoided, and citalopram itself is a recognised cause of dose-dependent QT prolongation.
options: Procainamide
Defibrillate
Potassium chloride 20 mEq/h IV
Cardiovert (synchronised)
Amiodarone

questions.question: Which of the following IV fluids are NOT recommended for use in sepsis resuscitation?
questions.explanation: Hydroxyethyl starch (HES) is specifically recommended against by the SSC due to associations with organ injury and increased mortality. Crystalloids (Plasmalyte, normal saline, Lactated Ringers) are recommended as first-line fluids for initial resuscitation — balanced crystalloids (Plasmalyte, LR) are preferred over normal saline. Albumin can be considered in addition to crystalloids, particularly in patients requiring substantial amounts of crystalloids.
options: Normal (0.9%) saline
Lactated Ringers solution
Albumin
Hydroxyethyl starch (HES)
Plasmalyte

questions.question: Regarding bedside investigations for a desaturating, mechanically ventilated polytrauma patient:
questions.explanation: Chest radiographs are quick and easy to obtain, but patients often must be imaged supine, which limits assessment of both pleural effusions and anterior pneumothoraces. Point-of-care ultrasound has high sensitivity and specificity for pneumothorax and effusion and can also guide therapeutic interventions such as drainage. CT scanning is the most detailed option but is lengthy and carries the risk of transferring an unstable patient off the unit with limited monitoring and potential for deterioration. Clinical examination is the quickest option but carries many limitations in the critically ill polytrauma patient.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Supine chest radiography reliably detects anterior pneumothoraces

statements.label: B
statements.text: Clinical examination alone has important limitations in the critically ill patient

statements.label: C
statements.text: Point-of-care ultrasound can also be used to guide therapeutic drainage of an effusion or pneumothorax

statements.label: D
statements.text: Computed tomography carries no additional risk compared with bedside investigations in an unstable patient

questions.question: In peripheral bifemoral veno-arterial ECMO...
questions.explanation: Peripheral VA-ECMO returns oxygenated blood retrograde into the aorta, increasing left ventricular afterload; this raises left ventricular end-diastolic pressure and can worsen pulmonary oedema (the rationale for LV venting strategies). An IABP is not contraindicated and may help offload the LV, and oxygenation should be monitored from the right upper limb (right radial artery), not the left, given the risk of differential (Harlequin) hypoxia.
options: Right ventricular preload will be increased
Left ventricular end diastolic pressure will be increased
Intra-aortic balloon pump use is contraindicated due to the disruption to flow
Oxygen saturations and blood gases should be monitored from the left upper limb

questions.question: The following are patient-reported outcome measures:
questions.explanation: Patient-reported outcome measures capture the patient's own assessment of health status or quality of life, such as quality of life and quality of recovery scores. Myocardial infarction is a clinician-diagnosed clinical event and critical care free days is a derived metric calculated from length-of-stay data — neither is reported directly by the patient.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Quality of life

statements.label: B
statements.text: Myocardial infarction

statements.label: C
statements.text: Critical care free days

statements.label: D
statements.text: Quality of recovery

questions.question: Sputum Gram stain is performed and shown below, alongside blood and sputum cultures sent for processing. What is the main diagnostic value of the Gram stain at this stage?
questions.explanation: Gram stain is quick, cheap and widely available, and gives an early read on Gram reaction and morphology (e.g. Gram-negative rods versus Gram-positive cocci) that can help focus empirical therapy before culture results return. It cannot reliably identify an organism to species level on morphology alone, does not detect resistance genes, cannot detect viruses, and does not replace culture and susceptibility testing, which remain necessary to confirm the pathogen and guide definitive therapy. Common causes of hospital-acquired pneumonia include Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, plus oral anaerobic flora such as Peptococcus and Peptostreptococcus species - the Gram stain narrows this differential but does not settle it on its own.
options: It replaces the need for culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing
It definitively identifies the causative organism to species level
It reliably detects antibiotic resistance genes
It provides rapid, broad information - Gram reaction and bacterial morphology - that can help narrow empirical therapy while culture results are awaited
It can identify viral pathogens contributing to the pneumonia

questions.question: The same 35-year-old man (intubated for ARDS due to Legionella pneumonia, on ceftriaxone and a macrolide) has an initial arterial blood gas of pH 7.27, PaCO2 50 mmHg, PaO2 75 mmHg on FiO2 1.0. The ventilator is now set to volume-controlled mode, tidal volume 7.5 ml/kg predicted body weight, PEEP 10 cmH2O, respiratory rate 20/min, with a plateau pressure of 26 cmH2O. Regarding the next steps, are the following statements true or false?
questions.explanation: PaO2/FiO2 = 75/1.0 = 75 mmHg, i.e. severe ARDS (≤100 mmHg) — not moderate (100–200 mmHg), so statement 2 is false and statement 1 is true. Plateau pressure (26 cmH2O) is comfortably below the 28–30 cmH2O safety ceiling, leaving room to increase PEEP further; the Briel et al. meta-analysis suggested a higher-PEEP strategy (≥15 cmH2O) may benefit patients with PaO2/FiO2 <200 mmHg, provided haemodynamics and plateau pressure are rechecked promptly (statement 3 true). The mild, compensated respiratory acidosis (pH 7.27) is not the priority issue here, so a modest tidal volume increase was not judged critical to avoid (statement 4 true).

statements.label: A
statements.text: Given the current plateau pressure, PEEP can reasonably be increased to 15 cmH2O.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Increasing the tidal volume to 8 ml/kg predicted body weight would be a reasonable option, since the mild respiratory acidosis is not the critical problem here.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The PaO2/FiO2 ratio specifically confirms moderate ARDS.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The PaO2/FiO2 ratio confirms a diagnosis of ARDS.

questions.question: In NAVA, delivered pressure equals the NAVA level times the electrical activity of the diaphragm. If the EAdi signal becomes unreliable and a pneumatic (flow or pressure) criterion is met first, what happens?
questions.explanation: NAVA triggering follows a 'first come, first served' rule - whichever criterion (EAdi or pneumatic) is met first triggers the breath - and with a persistent EAdi problem the ventilator reverts automatically to physician-set pressure support, so the patient is never left without a working trigger. The other options deny or misdescribe this backup.
options: The ventilator ignores the pneumatic trigger entirely and waits indefinitely for a valid EAdi signal to appear
The ventilator defaults to a fully controlled mode whenever EAdi signal quality is poor
The pneumatic criterion triggers it ('first come, first served'); a persistent EAdi failure reverts to pressure support
NAVA has no backup triggering mechanism when the EAdi signal is lost
The ventilator stops delivering breaths until the EAdi signal is restored

questions.question: A 32-year-old man with a severe asthma attack is admitted to the ED at 20:00 hrs. He is given steroids, inhaled beta-adrenergic drugs and inhaled anticholinergic therapy. After two hours of observation and treatment, his vital signs and arterial blood gases have not improved. On 10 litres of oxygen by open mask he now has: BP 140/70 mmHg, pulse 130/min, respiratory rate 28/min, audible wheeze, and is unable to speak in full sentences. ABG: pH 7.23, PaO2 10 kPa, PaCO2 7.9 kPa, HCO3 23 mmol/L, BE -2 mmol/L. What is your action at this time?
questions.explanation: [UNCONFIRMED] A progressive rise in PaCO2 despite optimal treatment for severe asthma is a sign of impending respiratory exhaustion and a predictor of fatal asthma, occurring even before severe hypercapnia develops. Such a patient should be transferred to ICU for close monitoring and early identification of the need for intubation, rather than committing immediately to intubation or remaining in a lower-acuity setting. No option letter or green check was shown by ESICM - inferred from feedback text stating the patient should be 'admitted in ICU for close monitoring and early identification for intubation need'.
options: Transfer to an intermediate care unit for further medical treatment
Transfer to the ICU for non-invasive ventilation
Transfer to an ICU for immediate intubation and IPPV
Transfer to an ICU for further observation
Keep the patient in the ED for another 2-3 hours

questions.question: Regarding risk stratification scoring systems in ACS:
questions.explanation: Describing the TIMI risk score for UA/NSTEMI as using 5 independent predictors is false — it actually uses 7 (age ≥65, ≥3 coronary risk factors, prior stenosis ≥50%, ST-segment deviation, ≥2 anginal events in 24 hours, elevated biomarkers, and prior aspirin use). A GRACE score above 140 identifying intermediate risk is false — a score that high identifies HIGH risk of in-hospital mortality; 109–140 is the intermediate band. The CRUSADE bleeding score including male sex as one of its 8 variables is false — it is FEMALE sex that counts toward bleeding risk, alongside baseline haematocrit, creatinine clearance, diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, heart failure signs, systolic blood pressure and heart rate. The GRACE score comprising age, heart rate, systolic blood pressure, serum creatinine, Killip class, cardiac arrest at admission, biomarker elevation and ST-segment deviation as its 8 components is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The TIMI risk score for UA/NSTEMI predicts 14-day risk of death, MI, or urgent revascularisation using 5 independent predictors

statements.label: B
statements.text: The CRUSADE bleeding score includes male sex as one of its 8 variables for NSTEMI in-hospital bleeding risk

statements.label: C
statements.text: The GRACE score includes age, heart rate, systolic BP, serum creatinine, Killip class, cardiac arrest, biomarker elevation, and ST deviation as its 8 components.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A GRACE score >140 identifies patients at intermediate (not high) risk of in-hospital mortality.

questions.question: Regarding post-traumatic meningitis in severe TBI, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE.
questions.explanation: Open wounds, CSF leaks, and EVDs are the main risk factors. CSF glucose <50 mg/dL IS a useful diagnostic criterion — along with WBC >10,000/mm³, protein >100 mg/dL, and high CSF lactate. Treatment must be immediate given high untreated mortality. Routine catheter replacement does NOT reduce infection risk and is not recommended.
questions.section: TBI Part V: Complications and Outcomes

statements.label: A
statements.text: CSF glucose below 50 mg/dL (2.8 mmol/L) is not a useful diagnostic criterion for bacterial meningitis

statements.label: B
statements.text: Risk factors include open skull fractures, CSF leaks via basal skull fractures, and ventricular drainage catheters

statements.label: C
statements.text: Post-traumatic bacterial meningitis requires immediate treatment as untreated disease carries high mortality

statements.label: D
statements.text: Routine scheduled replacement of ventricular catheters effectively prevents catheter-associated ventriculitis

questions.question: Regarding risk factors for difficult and prolonged weaning from recent studies:
questions.explanation: Immunocompromised patients having notably higher rates of weaning failure, and older age and frailty being strong predictors of weaning failure in the WEAN SAFE study, are both accurately described findings. The claim that surgical patients generally have higher extubation-failure rates than medical patients is false and reversed — medical patients actually had extubation-failure rates above 20% while surgical patients were below 10%. The claim that chronic cardiac failure present on admission has been associated with worse weaning outcomes is also false and reversed — chronic cardiac failure on admission was, counterintuitively, associated with better outcomes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Chronic cardiac failure present on admission has been associated with worse weaning outcomes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Immunocompromised patients have notably higher rates of weaning failure.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Surgical patients generally have higher extubation-failure rates than medical patients.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Older age and frailty are strong predictors of weaning failure in the WEAN SAFE study.

questions.question: A nutrition team is reviewing predictive equations for energy expenditure in obese ICU patients (BMI >30 kg/m²). They note that most equations perform poorly in this group. Which predictive equation is an exception and shows better performance in obese critically ill patients?
questions.explanation: Most predictive equations for energy expenditure perform poorly in obese patients (BMI >30 kg/m²) and substantially over- or underestimate energy needs. The Penn State equation was specifically developed and validated for obese critically ill patients and incorporates minute ventilation and maximum body temperature over the preceding 24 hours in addition to anthropometric data. Even so, clinical judgment remains essential, and indirect calorimetry remains the gold standard when available and technically feasible.
options: Schofield equation
Harris-Benedict equation
Penn State equation
Ireton-Jones equation
Mifflin-St Jeor equation

questions.question: Adrenomedullin has been implicated in the pathophysiology of sepsis causing vasodilation and capillary leakage. Adrecizumab has been developed to counteract this pathophysiology in the management of sepsis. Please choose true/false of the following statements regarding Adrenomedullin and Adrecizumab:
questions.explanation: Adrenomedullin (ADM) is elevated in BOTH septic AND cardiogenic shock. Intravascularly, ADM protects the endothelial barrier at tight junctions; when it leaks extravascularly due to inflammation, it causes vasodilation. Adrecizumab is a humanised NON-blocking antibody that binds to the N-terminal segment of ADM, making it too large a molecule to leak out of the endothelium, thereby decreasing extravascular concentration and enhancing intravascular action. The half-life is PROLONGED from 20 min to 15 days (Adrecizumab PROLONGS, not decreases, the half-life). Adrecizumab is NON-blocking — it does NOT prevent ADM binding to its receptor.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adrecizumab is a blocking antibody thereby preventing its binding to its receptor

statements.label: B
statements.text: Extravascular adrenomedullin causes systemic vasodilation, but intravascular adrenomedullin protects endothelial barrier

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adrecizumab decreases half-life of adrenomedullin thus mitigating systemic vasodilation

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adrenomedullin is elevated in septic shock and not in cardiogenic shock

questions.question: An intubated 55-year-old patient with known alcohol use disorder develops unexplained hypoxic respiratory failure and haemodynamic instability with no clear septic source. Serum amylase is within normal limits. Which of the following statements about this result is LEAST accurate?
questions.explanation: Normal serum amylase does not exclude acute pancreatitis — it is within normal limits at admission in approximately 20% of attacks. Serum lipase is more sensitive, more disease-specific, and should be measured in all suspected cases. A high index of suspicion must be maintained in unconscious patients or those with unexplained organ failure and alcohol or gallstone history. In renal failure, impaired amylase clearance can produce false-positive elevations. The least accurate statement is that normal amylase reliably excludes the diagnosis.
options: In patients with renal failure, elevated amylase may represent a false positive due to impaired clearance
Normal serum amylase reliably excludes acute pancreatitis in patients without pre-existing chronic pancreatic disease
Normal serum amylase occurs in up to 20% of acute pancreatitis attacks at admission and lipase should be measured
Serum lipase is more sensitive and disease-specific than amylase and remains elevated for longer
A high index of suspicion for pancreatitis is warranted in unconscious patients with alcohol history and unexplained organ failure

questions.question: A 37 year old fire fighter is admitted to the ICU with an inhalation injury after prolonged smoke exposure during a fire rescue. She was found to have soot on her skin, nares and oral mucosa but no evidence of a burn injury. On arrival to the Emergency Department she was intubated due to respiratory distress. Co-oximetry confirmed carboxyhaemoglobin levels 41%. She was transferred to the ICU with SpO2 100% on FiO2 1.0 with diffuse bilateral changes on chest x-ray. The nursing staff note carbonaceous sputum on endotracheal aspirate. Which of the following statements are true?
questions.explanation: Bronchoscopy has an important prognostic role in confirming diagnosis and grading inhalation injury, but bronchial interventions such as lavage or inhaled therapies - including nebulised N-Acetyl Cysteine and heparin - lack a robust evidence base to support routine therapeutic use. Pulse oximetry measures combined oxy- and carboxyhaemoglobin saturation, so SpO2 can read normal despite severe carbon monoxide poisoning - a falsely reassuring finding. Tracheobronchial injury is most commonly due to inhaled particulate matter or chemicals rather than direct thermal injury, since hot air cools rapidly before reaching the lower airway.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Treatment of severe / massive tracheobronchial injury with nebulised N-Acetyl Cysteine and heparin has a strong evidence base

statements.label: B
statements.text: Fibreoptic bronchoscopy has both an important prognostic and therapeutic role in inhalation injury

statements.label: C
statements.text: Tracheobronchial injury is most commonly caused by thermal injury to the bronchial tree

statements.label: D
statements.text: Peripheral oxygen saturations may be normal in cases of severe carbon monoxide poisoning

questions.question: Besides directly raising transpulmonary pressure and tidal volume, how else can vigorous spontaneous breathing promote pulmonary oedema in an injured lung?
questions.explanation: Negative intrathoracic pressure from vigorous effort raises venous return and the transmural pressure of the pulmonary vessels, favouring oedema - an additional P-SILI mechanism alongside pendelluft. The other options reverse or deny the mechanism.
options: By reducing cardiac output to zero, removing all pulmonary vascular pressure change
By a mechanism that has never been proposed in the literature
By lowering venous return and reducing pulmonary vascular pressures
By directly causing bronchospasm, unrelated to any vascular mechanism
Negative intrathoracic pressure raises venous return and vascular transmural pressure

questions.question: Regarding meropenem:
questions.explanation: Meropenem is a carbapenem (a beta-lactam) with one of the broadest spectrums of any antibacterial, covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms (though not MRSA or Enterococcus faecium, and some Pseudomonas strains are meropenem-resistant). Cross-sensitivity with penicillin is possible but not absolute - a patient with a history of a mild reaction such as rash should not automatically be excluded from meropenem if it is strongly indicated. Being relatively time-dependent in its killing (a T>MIC of at least 40% is needed), PK/PD targets for meropenem are better achieved with extended or continuous infusion, and dosing requires reduction as glomerular filtration falls, including in renal replacement therapy. (Peck, Hill & Williams, Pharmacology for Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, 2nd ed., 2006, p. 311; Thirunavakkarasu & Lynch, Anaesthesia Tutorial of the Week 2010;168)

statements.label: A
statements.text: It is a beta-lactam antibiotic

statements.label: B
statements.text: It is absolutely contraindicated in patients with a penicillin allergy

statements.label: C
statements.text: It has a spectrum that does not cover anaerobes

statements.label: D
statements.text: It can be used as a continuous or extended infusion in septic patients

questions.question: Regarding sodium nitroprusside and its toxicity:
questions.explanation: Describing cyanide toxicity as presenting with metabolic lactic acidosis, confusion and cardiovascular deterioration is true — these are the 'hard' signs requiring immediate intervention. Citing a sodium thiosulphate dose of 15 mg/kg IV as the treatment is false — the correct dose is 150 mg/kg IV; a 10-fold underdose would be inadequate to convert accumulating cyanide to thiocyanate. Claiming nitroprusside remains first-line in acute MI is false — it is no longer used there because of coronary steal risk, with nitroglycerin preferred instead. Describing thiocyanate toxicity as presenting similarly to cyanide toxicity (lactic acidosis, cardiovascular collapse) is false — thiocyanate toxicity instead causes abdominal pain, delirium, headache, nausea, muscle spasms and restlessness.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Thiocyanate toxicity typically presents with lactic acidosis and cardiovascular collapse, similar to cyanide toxicity

statements.label: B
statements.text: Sodium thiosulphate 15 mg/kg IV converts cyanide to thiocyanate and is a key treatment for nitroprusside-induced cyanide toxicity

statements.label: C
statements.text: Sodium nitroprusside remains first-line in acute myocardial infarction because its rapid onset outweighs any theoretical coronary steal risk

statements.label: D
statements.text: Cyanide toxicity from nitroprusside typically presents with metabolic lactic acidosis, confusion and haemodynamic deterioration

questions.question: A patient with acute ischaemic stroke is eligible for intravenous thrombolysis. The patient weighs 80 kg. What is the correct total dose of alteplase (rt-PA) and the appropriate administration regimen?
questions.explanation: The standard dose of alteplase for acute ischaemic stroke is 0.9 mg/kg with a maximum of 90 mg (for patients ≥100 kg). Ten percent of the total dose is administered as an immediate IV bolus, and the remaining 90% is infused continuously over one hour. For an 80 kg patient: 0.9 × 80 = 72 mg total. The distractor that omits the bolus entirely is wrong, as is the one applying the 90 mg cap regardless of weight — a clinically plausible trap if one forgets that dosing is weight-based below 100 kg.
options: 90 mg (maximum dose regardless of weight); 10% IV bolus then remainder over 60 minutes
72 mg (0.9 mg/kg); administered entirely as a continuous infusion over 60 minutes
0.6 mg/kg (48 mg); 10% as IV bolus, remainder over 60 minutes
1.0 mg/kg (80 mg, max 100 mg); administered as continuous infusion over 90 minutes
0.9 mg/kg (≈72 mg); 10% as immediate IV bolus, remaining 90% as continuous infusion over 60 minutes

questions.question: Regarding practical management of patients with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs):
questions.explanation: A magnet over the ICD generator deactivating defibrillation function is correct, as is the ability to use external defibrillation while avoiding placement directly over the device, and the ability to interrogate the device for arrhythmic episode data. Claiming a magnet also stops pacing function is false: the magnet specifically deactivates tachyarrhythmia (shock) therapy, while the device's pacing function for bradycardia continues to operate normally.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A magnet placed over an ICD generator also stops any pacing function the device provides.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Standard external defibrillation paddles or pads can still be used in a patient with an ICD in place, but should not be placed directly over the device.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Placing a magnet directly over the ICD generator deactivates its defibrillation function.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Modern ICDs can be interrogated to determine the number and duration of arrhythmic episodes that have occurred.

questions.question: A polytrauma patient in the ICU, mechanically ventilated, develops a sudden desaturation to SpO2 80%. Which investigation is most likely to give the quickest, most reliable information?
questions.explanation: Point-of-care ultrasound has high sensitivity and specificity for both pneumothorax and pleural effusion, can be performed immediately at the bedside, and can also guide therapeutic drainage. Clinical examination is quickest but has many limitations in the critically ill. Chest radiography is quick but the need for a supine view limits assessment of effusions and anterior pneumothoraces. CT is the most detailed but is lengthy and carries risks from transferring an unstable patient off the unit with limited monitoring. Arterial blood gas can confirm hypoxaemia but does not localise its cause.
options: Clinical examination (auscultation and inspection) alone
Supine chest radiograph
Point-of-care ultrasound
Computed tomography with transfer off the unit
Arterial blood gas analysis alone

questions.question: The conflict management framework shown identifies five domains for addressing conflicts in the ICU. Which of the following is NOT one of the recognised domains in this framework?
questions.explanation: The conflict management framework comprises five domains: (1) Clear communication — open channels, active listening, structured tools such as the COMFORT model; (2) Multidisciplinary team collaboration — involving physicians, nurses, social workers, ethicists; (3) Ethical and mediating consultations — ethics committees, trained mediators — not legal department referral; (4) Family meetings and support — involvement in rounds, emotional support, clear information sharing; (5) Advance care planning — early goals-of-care discussions to preempt conflict. Immediate legal referral is not a first-line strategy; it is potentially escalatory and is not part of this evidence-based framework.
questions.section: Conflicts in the intensive care unit
options: Family meetings and emotional support for patients' families
Referring all unresolved conflicts immediately to the hospital legal department for binding adjudication
Clear communication with open and transparent channels among all parties
Multidisciplinary team collaboration in decision-making processes
Advance care planning initiated early in the ICU admission process

questions.question: Which of the following ECG patterns is consistent with those seen in the setting of non-ST elevation myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation: ALL of the above are consistent with NSTE-ACS. ECG changes include: ST depression (transient or persistent), T-wave inversion, ST elevation (transient), or a NORMAL ECG (occurs in 1-6% of NSTE-ACS patients). A normal ECG does NOT exclude ACS. Wellen's phenomenon (biphasic/deeply inverted T waves in anterior leads) indicates critical proximal LAD stenosis. If ECG is non-diagnostic, repeat at 15-30 min intervals, especially if symptoms recur.
options: Normal ST segments and T waves
Down-sloping ST segment depression
All of the above
Wellen's phenomenon (biphasic or deeply inverted T waves in the anterior precordial leads)
Isolated T wave flattening or inversion

questions.question: A hospital executive proposes using shorter ICU length of stay (LOS) as the main quality indicator. As an intensivist, you are asked to comment on the plan. What is the single best statement?
questions.explanation: ICU length of stay reflects resource utilisation but is confounded by case complexity, discharge practices, and post-ICU resource availability. Pursuing shorter LOS as a primary target risks premature discharge and increased readmission or other adverse events - it does not directly measure patient-centred recovery or isolate ICU-specific performance.
options: ICU readmissions indicate premature discharge and therefore better suited to measure ICU quality.
ICU LOS is a proxy for resource use, but shorter LOS may be associated with higher readmission or other adverse events.
ICU LOS is unaffected by case complexity or post-ICU resources, so it isolates ICU performance.
ICU LOS directly measures patient-centred recovery and long-term functional independence.
Shorter ICU LOS improves outcomes without increased complications.

questions.question: A 55-year-old mechanically ventilated patient has persistent high gastric residual volumes (>500 mL/6h) on two consecutive measurements despite reducing the feed rate and elevating the head of bed to 30 degrees. What is the recommended first-line prokinetic agent and dose?
questions.explanation: Erythromycin 250 mg IV every 6 hours is the recommended first-line prokinetic agent for high gastric residual volumes in ICU patients. Erythromycin acts as a motilin receptor agonist and accelerates gastric emptying. Metoclopramide (10 mg IV every 8 hours) is a second-line option and has a maximum recommended duration of 5 days due to the risk of extrapyramidal side effects, including tardive dyskinesia. Cisapride is no longer available in most countries due to cardiac arrhythmia risk. Domperidone and neostigmine are not standard first-line agents for gastric EN intolerance.
options: Cisapride 10 mg nasogastrically three times daily
Neostigmine 2.5 mg IV every 6 hours
Domperidone 10 mg nasogastrically every 8 hours
Erythromycin 250 mg IV every 6 hours
Metoclopramide 10 mg IV every 8 hours

questions.question: Which of the following adjunctive therapies for sepsis is presently recommended based upon available clinical evidence?
questions.explanation: DVT prophylaxis with heparins (LMWH preferably, or UFH) is strongly recommended for septic patients in the absence of contraindications. Sepsis is a risk factor for VTE especially with hypotension, shock, and vasopressor use. SSC 2021 suggests against IVIG (weak recommendation). Intensive glucose control (90-120 mg/dL) is harmful (NICE-SUGAR) — target is ≤180 mg/dL. The SSC issued a strong recommendation against erythropoietin. The SSC 2016 guidelines suggest prophylactic platelets at <10,000/mm³ (absent bleeding) or <20,000/mm³ with significant haemorrhage risk; most recent guidelines make no recommendations regarding platelet transfusions.
options: Deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis with heparins (unfractionated or low-molecular weight, in the absence of haemorrhage)
Platelet transfusions should be given when the platelet count is below 50,000/mm³
Erythropoietin administration for sepsis-associated anaemia with haemoglobin levels <7 g/dL
Intravenous immunoglobulin in patients with vasopressors refractory septic shock
Intensive glucose control, with blood glucose targets of 90-120 mg/dL (5-6.7 mmol/L)

questions.question: For which of the following patients does the WHO strongly recommend urine lipoarabinomannan (LAM) lateral flow assay as a point-of-care TB screening test?
questions.explanation: The WHO strongly recommends the urine LAM assay for HIV-positive adults and children with a CD4 count below 100/mm³, and for those who are seriously ill and hospitalised regardless of clinical TB symptoms. The patient with CD4 88/mm³ who is seriously ill and hospitalised meets both criteria. Patients with CD4 counts of 340/mm³ or 150/mm³ exceed the relevant CD4 threshold and are not described as seriously ill, so they do not meet the recommendation. An HIV-negative patient is not an indication for this test at all. Extending the recommendation to any hospitalised patient regardless of HIV status goes too far, since LAM sensitivity is substantially lower in the absence of HIV-associated immunosuppression.
options: An HIV-positive 40-year-old with CD4 count 88/mm³ who is seriously ill and hospitalised
Any hospitalised patient from a high-incidence TB country, regardless of HIV status
An HIV-positive outpatient with CD4 count 340/mm³ presenting with a 6-week cough
An HIV-positive 38-year-old with CD4 count 150/mm³ detected incidentally on screening
An HIV-negative 55-year-old from a TB-endemic country admitted with suspected pneumonia

questions.question: A 42 year-old woman with a past medical history of HIV is admitted with progressively worsening shortness of breath and malaise. She also complains of fever, chills, wheezing, and cough with yellow sputum. She is intermittently compliant with her cHART therapy and her CD4+ cell count is 75/uL. Chest CT is shown. The patient should be started on.
questions.explanation: Patients with HIV have a predictable pattern of susceptibility to infections determined by their CD4+ count, and this patient's CD4+ count of 75/uL puts her at risk of fungal infections. Her chest CT shows a pulmonary nodule with surrounding ground-glass opacity (the "halo sign"), typically seen in angio-invasive Aspergillosis. She should be started on empiric voriconazole pending testing for Aspergillus.
options: Voriconazole
Acyclovir
Ampicillin
Ceftriaxone
Vancomycin and Cefepime

questions.question: What is the diagnosis of septic shock based on?
questions.explanation: Septic shock (Sepsis-3) is defined as a subset of sepsis with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg AND serum lactate >2 mmol/L (18 mg/dL) despite adequate volume resuscitation. It requires the presence of sepsis. Positive blood cultures are not required — diagnosis is clinical. Lactate >2 mmol/L is required. Vasopressors are needed *despite* adequate fluid resuscitation, not *before* it — so requiring vasopressors before fluid resuscitation is therefore false.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Serum lactate >2 mmol/L

statements.label: B
statements.text: Positive blood cultures for a known pathogen

statements.label: C
statements.text: Need for vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure >65 mmHg before fluid resuscitation

statements.label: D
statements.text: The presence of sepsis

questions.question: A patient with an inferior STEMI develops the rhythm strip shown, with a ventricular rate of 32 bpm and a wide QRS escape rhythm. Atropine 1 mg IV is given, but the ventricular rate does not improve and appears to fall further. What is the most likely explanation, and what should be done next?
questions.explanation: This rhythm strip shows complete (third-degree) AV block: P waves and QRS complexes occur independently of each other (AV dissociation), with a wide QRS indicating a slow, infranodal escape rhythm. Atropine can paradoxically appear to worsen block when the escape rhythm arises from infranodal tissue: it increases the sinus firing rate via vagal blockade but has little effect on the infranodal focus itself, so the block appears unchanged or worse. The appropriate next step is a chronotropic infusion (dopamine, epinephrine, or isoproterenol) while arranging transvenous pacing, using transcutaneous pacing as a bridge if needed. Simply repeating atropine, blaming vagal overstimulation, or doubting a well-supported diagnosis all misunderstand the mechanism, and atropine is an appropriate (if sometimes ineffective) first-line agent, not a contraindicated one.
options: The escape rhythm is infranodal (His-Purkinje) in origin; atropine increases the sinus rate without affecting the infranodal focus, so a chronotropic infusion or pacing is needed instead
Atropine has caused paradoxical vagal stimulation and should be reversed with glycopyrrolate
Atropine is contraindicated in complete heart block and should never have been given

This indicates the rhythm is not truly complete heart block, and the diagnosis should be reconsidered in light of the persistent bradycardia despite an adequate dose of atropine having already been administered
The dose of atropine was too low; repeat atropine up to a cumulative dose of 3 mg

questions.question: A 58-year-old 90kg man was admitted with a 2-day history of pyrexia, urinary incontinence and abdominal pain. His past medical history included hypertension, kidney stones and a recent course of ciprofloxacin for urinary tract infection. Blood results showed an acute rise in serum creatinine to 2.5 times his baseline. His fractional excretion of sodium was 4% and coarse granular casts on urine microscopy. The urine dipstick did not show haematuria, leukocyturia or proteinuria. There were no red cell casts, white cell casts or eosinophil. The most likely pathophysiology is:
questions.explanation: Sepsis-induced AKI is the most likely cause. The patient presents with fever, urinary tract symptoms and abdominal pain consistent with sepsis. He showed no signs of dehydration, making hypovolaemia unlikely. There was no history of urinary retention or renal colic to suggest obstruction. Urine dipstick did not show haematuria, leukocyturia or proteinuria, making glomerulonephritis and interstitial nephritis unlikely. High FENa (4%) is consistent with intrinsic renal injury from sepsis.
options: Sepsis
Urinary tract obstruction
Hypovolaemia
Acute glomerulonephritis
Acute interstitial nephritis

questions.question: Regarding the global epidemiology of AKI:
questions.explanation: Global AKI incidence is measured broadly across hospitalised patients (about 1 in 5 adults, 1 in 3 children), not confined to ICU populations. Only 10–15% of ICU patients with AKI require RRT, not the majority; the AKI-EPI study found adjusted risks of AKI and mortality were similar across continents rather than showing regional disparity.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In the ICU, the incidence of AKI varies between one-third and two-thirds of patients depending on the criteria and population studied.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The adjusted risk of AKI and associated mortality was similar across different continents and regions in the AKI-EPI study.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A meta-analysis found that the majority of AKI cases worldwide are diagnosed only in ICU patients, with negligible incidence on general hospital wards.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Of all ICU patients with AKI, the majority (>50%) require renal replacement therapy.

questions.question: Two EEG records from patients with altered consciousness are shown (see image). Record A shows continuous rhythmic activity with sharp and polysharp waves and spatial-temporal organisation. Record B shows 2-3 Hz slow activity with fluctuating triphasic waves maximal over anterior regions and inconstant reactivity to stimulation. Which diagnoses correspond to Records A and B respectively?
questions.explanation: Record A shows hallmarks of electrographic status epilepticus: continuous rhythmic sharp and polysharp waves with spatial-temporal organisation and no reactivity. Record B shows the characteristic hepatic encephalopathy pattern: slow 2-3 Hz activity with fluctuating triphasic waves frontally and inconstant reactivity. Distinguishing these patterns is clinically critical: status epilepticus demands urgent antiepileptic treatment, while the hepatic pattern redirects management toward liver dysfunction. PLEDs are a distinct entity associated with acutely destructive processes.
options: A = herpes simplex encephalitis; B = uraemic encephalopathy
A = hepatic encephalopathy; B = non-convulsive status epilepticus
A = burst-suppression; B = periodic lateralised epileptiform discharges
A = non-convulsive status epilepticus; B = hepatic encephalopathy
Both records are non-specifically consistent with septic encephalopathy

questions.question: The 'long-term' outcomes refer to patient status after the immediate postoperative period. Typically this will be X days after surgery, where X is:
questions.explanation: Long-term postoperative outcomes are conventionally defined as status beyond the acute 30-day window, which is also the standard timeframe used for surgical mortality and morbidity reporting. Shorter intervals capture only the immediate in-hospital course, while longer intervals are used less commonly as the primary long-term benchmark.
options: 5 days
30 days
15 days
90 days
60 days

questions.question: Which ONE of the following statements describes a patient with a myocardial infarction that is Killip Class IV?
questions.explanation: Killip Class IV = cardiogenic shock: SBP < 90 mmHg plus signs of hypoperfusion (oliguria, cyanosis, sweating). Mortality ~81% in original 1967 data. Class I = no HF (mortality 6%), Class II = mild-moderate HF with S3/rales < halfway/elevated JVP (mortality 17%), Class III = pulmonary oedema (mortality 38%). Mortality rates have declined 30-50% with modern reperfusion therapy.
options: No evidence of heart failure. Arterial capillary pressure < 15-18 mmHg Cardiac Index > 2,2 l/min/m2
Pulmonary oedema. Arterial capillary pressure > 18 mmHg Cardiac Index > 2,2 l/min/m2
Hypotension and bradycardia in the evolution of a inferior STEMI
Findings of mild to moderate heart failure (S3 gallop, rales < half-way up lung fields or elevated jugular venous pressure)
Cardiogenic shock defined as systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg and signs of hypoperfusion such as oliguria, cyanosis and sweating

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with pneumococcal septic shock develops progressive coagulopathy. Which combination of laboratory findings is most consistent with overt DIC?
questions.explanation: Typical DIC laboratory findings are: prolonged PT (reflecting consumption of coagulation factors), prolonged aPTT, thrombocytopenia (platelet consumption in microthrombi), elevated fibrin-related markers (D-dimer/FDP, reflecting fibrinolysis of fibrin clots), and reduced fibrinogen (consumed in fibrin formation). An isolated aPTT prolongation, isolated thrombocytopenia, or normal PT with markedly elevated fibrinogen are not consistent with DIC. Note that these findings resemble advanced liver disease, making the underlying clinical context essential.
options: Normal PT, prolonged aPTT, normal platelet count, markedly elevated fibrinogen, and low D-dimer
Normal PT and aPTT, markedly elevated platelet count, elevated fibrinogen, and mildly elevated D-dimer
Markedly prolonged PT, normal aPTT, thrombocytopenia, low D-dimer, and markedly elevated fibrinogen
Prolonged PT, prolonged aPTT, thrombocytopenia, elevated D-dimer/FDP, and low fibrinogen
Isolated thrombocytopenia with normal PT, normal aPTT, normal fibrinogen, and normal D-dimer

questions.question: An example of a process measure includes:
questions.explanation: Process measures assess how care is delivered rather than its clinical result, so length of hospital stay reflects care delivery and resource use rather than a clinical endpoint. Mortality, morbidity, pneumonia incidence, and lung function tests all capture the result of care and are therefore outcome measures, not process measures.
questions.section: Outcome measurement: process vs outcome measures
options: Postoperative morbidity
Incidence of postoperative pneumonia
Length of hospital stay
Lung function tests
In-hospital mortality

questions.question: The following are indications for surgery in a patient with acute severe pancreatitis:
questions.explanation: Undisputed indications for surgery include severe retroperitoneal haemorrhage and acute abdomen (peritonitis). When percutaneous/other drainage techniques have been unsuccessful or not indicated, surgery is indicated for abdominal compartment syndrome and drainage of infected pancreatic necrosis. In case of biliary obstruction with failed endoscopic access to the bile duct, percutaneous drainage is favoured over surgery. Surgery for sterile pancreatic necrosis inevitably leads to further complications, such as infection, and is no longer recommended. Cholecystectomy should be delayed until 4-6 weeks after the episode to allow inflammation to subside. Reference: ESICM PACT Module Acute Pancreatitis.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Peritonitis

statements.label: B
statements.text: Cholecystectomy during acute attack

statements.label: C
statements.text: Sterile pancreatic necrosis

statements.label: D
statements.text: Severe retroperitoneal haemorrhage
